China. One of the world's oldest continuous civilizations, spanning over four thousand years of recorded history. From the earliest dynasties through imperial periods that ruled vast territories, to the modern communist state under Mao and beyond, China has been a center of philosophy, art, governance, and technological innovation.

China's written history begins with the Shang dynasty around sixteen hundred to ten forty-six BCE, and its classical period culminated in the Han dynasty from two hundred six BCE to two hundred twenty CE, which established many institutions that lasted millennia. The Great Wall of China, built over centuries from the seventh century BCE onward, was intended to defend against invasions from the north and symbolizes Chinese engineering and ambition. The Silk Road, a network of trade routes from the second century BCE onward, connected China to Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, facilitating commerce, ideas, and religions including Buddhism.

Confucianism and Taoism, philosophical and spiritual systems developed in ancient China, profoundly shaped East Asian ethics, governance, and personal practice for millennia. The Forbidden City in Beijing, built in the fifteenth century, was the imperial palace for nearly five hundred years and exemplifies classical Chinese architecture and court hierarchy. Mao Zedong, from eighteen ninety-three to nineteen seventy-six, unified China as a communist state in nineteen forty-nine and ruled with revolutionary and devastating policies that reshaped the nation.

Chinese innovations—papermaking, printing, gunpowder, the compass—were exported globally and revolutionized technology and knowledge transmission. Confucianism shaped Chinese governance and society for twenty-five hundred years, while Taoism explores harmony with nature and the Tao. Buddhism entered China via the Silk Road and became deeply integrated, and Kung Fu, the martial art tradition, has deep roots in Chinese philosophy and monasticism.
